final.title: When AI scope starts to wander, draw the box first
final.body:
If you are looking at one recurring task and the scope keeps expanding, that is usually the warning sign.

A simple example: customer email replies, invoice handling, or lead follow-up can start as one workflow and quietly turn into five. The early sign of unbounded scope is not complexity. It is when the task stops having a clear input, a clear output, and a clear owner.

Before you automate or delegate it, write the boundary in plain English:
- what comes in
- what decision gets made
- what goes out
- what stays with a human

That last line matters. Money movement and other high-risk decisions stay human-approved.

If you cannot describe the workflow in one paragraph, it is not ready for automation yet. It probably needs restructuring first, or it may be better handled by hiring. Small box, fewer surprises. That is not a bad trade.

A practical next step: pick one recurring workflow and write a three-question check before any build: Is it repeated often enough? Are the rules clear? Can a wrong answer be caught before it reaches a customer or creates a risk? If the answer is yes, the scope is probably bounded enough to test. If not, keep the box smaller.

final.title: When AI scope starts to wander, define the box first
final.body:
If you are a small-business owner and an AI idea starts to sound useful, the first question is not “can we use AI?” It is: what exact workflow are we trying to automate?

Early signs of unbounded scope usually show up when the conversation slides from one repeatable task into a vague business wish. “Handle customer emails” is a workflow. “Improve customer experience” is not. One has inputs, outputs, and a boundary. The other can swallow the whole business.

A simple rule helps. Before you price or build anything, write three lines:
1) what goes in,
2) what decision the system may make,
3) what comes out.

Then add the human gate. If money movement, customer commitments, or another high-risk choice is involved, approval stays human. That is not a detail to patch in later; it is part of the scope.

If those three lines stay clear, you may have a bounded pilot. If they do not, the work needs restructuring first, or it is probably better solved by hiring or staying manual. The box is cheaper to draw on paper than in code.
